articles.title: Aardman at 50: Gromit was nearly a cat, Shaun the Sheep almost spoke
articles.summary: Aardman turns 50 with stories of cat-like Gromit, silent Shaun and Chicken Run's Oscar legacy.
articles.body:
Gromit was almost a cat. Shaun the Sheep was nearly given a voice. And Chicken Run helped change the Oscars forever.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story.

Founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976, Aardman has given us Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, the world's most successful stop-motion film.

But the journey from two teenagers "mucking about with plasticine" to an Oscar-winning animation powerhouse has often hinged on chance decisions, practical compromises and creative instinct.

Wallace and Gromit became Aardman's most famous characters after animator Nick Park joined the studio in 1985.

"I had this idea of an English guy who builds a rocket, in the basement of his house," recalled Park.

"I was thinking he may have a pet, probably a cat."

"I started modelling the cat, and it was just very difficult, so I thought I'd do a dog instead!"

Park was developing A Grand Day Out at the National Film and Television School in London when Lord and Sproxton came to speak to students.

"We met him and thought, 'Oh, he's good'. In fact, he's very good. Now I know him, he's actually a genius," said Lord.

The combination was electric. A Grand Day Out was nominated for an Oscar in 1990, losing only to another Aardman production, Creature Comforts, also directed by Park.

Pointing to a poster of Wallace and Gromit floating over Bristol in a hot-air balloon, Lord reflected on their appeal.

"When they appear on the screen, you laugh before they do anything."

Park later won three more Oscars. Perhaps it was just as well he never mastered Gromit the Cat.

By the mid-1990s, Wallace and Gromit had made Aardman one of the most talked-about names in animation.

That success led to an unlikely meeting with Steven Spielberg.

At dinner with Spielberg and DreamWorks chief executive Jeffrey Katzenberg, they pitched what became Chicken Run.

"We want to do The Great Escape," Lord told Spielberg.

"I had always been a fan of Aardman," Katzenberg said. "And I had this secret ambition that someday there would be a way to work together."

"Spielberg said, 'The Great Escape is one of my favourite films, and I have 300 chickens on my ranch!' So it went very well."

No-one had ever made a 90-minute stop-motion feature from modelling clay. The budget was more than £20m, and Aardman insisted every frame would be shot in Bristol.

The gamble paid off. Chicken Run took more than $220m (£165m) worldwide and remains the highest-grossing stop-motion film ever made.

At the time there was no Academy Award for animated features.

"And so because they couldn't give Chicken Run a little golden man, they invented the category," said Radio 1 film critic Ali Plumb.

The Academy introduced the Best Animated Feature Oscar the following year.

"And a couple of years later, Wallace and Gromit won that Oscar for 'The Curse of the Were-Rabbit', so they got their own reward," Plumb said.

If Chicken Run proved Aardman could conquer Hollywood, another character would go on to conquer the world.

Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest global stars.

Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions.

"The beauty of Shaun is it transcends borders and cultures because it doesn't rely on the spoken word," said Aardman's Managing Director Sean Clarke.

"You can literally see Shaun the Sheep here in Bristol and in Outer Mongolia."

Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice.

"When we launched the Shaun the Sheep series, we were told to add voices," Clarke remembered.

The same argument resurfaced when Shaun got his own feature film in 2015.

"They said, 'You can't do 80 minutes without any dialogue'.

"But we stuck to our convictions, and I think it is now one of our most revered films."

Lord insists Shaun was not kept silent to boost international sales, it simply "seemed better that way".

However, the character's global appeal is undeniable. Clarke said Shaun has been sold into 170 countries and is especially popular in Asia.

"Shaun is actually our most valuable character now.

"Wallace and Gromit built the house, but Shaun keeps the lights on."

It is a remarkable journey for a company that started almost by accident.

Lord and Sproxton began while still at school, "playing with Dad's cine camera", as Sproxton remembered.

Their first character was a 'superhero dolt', with a cape and a habit of falling down holes.

"We just thought 'Aardvark' was a silly word, so we combined it with 'Superman', he explained.

To their surprise, their short cartoon was bought by the BBC Bristol TV programme, 'Vision On'.

"They asked us who to make the cheque out to," recalled Lord with a fond smile.

If that cheque gave them a company name, their next creation gave them a star.

Lord and Sproxton moved to Bristol to work on Take Hart, the successor to Vision On.

On this show they took what Lord called "a leap into the third dimension".

"The budgets were low, and you can work quickly with it."

Soon he had fashioned Morph, the simple little terracotta brown figure that can change shape into anything, hence his name.

"It was just so easy to squash him up and reform him as a dog, or a submarine, or a bird or anything," Lord said.

Morph became a hit with children and parents alike, and remains a fixture at Aardman's Bristol headquarters.

Back in 1989, Lord told a BBC West documentary The Animators he "hoped Morph will still be around in 30 years or so, and still be loved."

It has been 37 years since he said that, and an Aardman exhibition at Bristol's MShed Museum was recently packed with Morph superfans.

But Lord, now the studio's creative director, still comes into the office and playfully reshapes Morph while chatting.

I asked him what Wallace would make of it all.

"Oh, he'd probably just say 'Cracking careers lads!'" he smiled.

articles.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing soars over Scottish coast
articles.summary: A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving with a broken wing has been spotted back above Scotland's west coast.
articles.body:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".

The bird, affectionately nicknamed Kinky because of the kink in its broken wing, was nursed back to health by its two, unusually caring parents.

In an unprecedented display of extended parenting, the two white-tailed parents skipped a year's breeding season to continue to tend for their year-old offspring.

This latest sighting, though, reveals that the bird survived his first winter alone.

The bird was photographed flying over Loch Spelve, a sea loch on the south-east coast of Mull.

Dave Sexton said: "I'm in awe of this bird!"

But the next phase of its life - which he described as a "sub-adult" could be dangerous.

"He'll no longer be tolerated as an immature by established adult pairs and might well come in for some 'you're not welcome here' behaviour, which can be pretty severe sometimes.

"But Kinky's a born survivor; I'm keeping everything crossed for him," he said.

Sea eagles, also known as white tailed eagles, were hunted to extinction in the UK and the UK's last native white-tailed eagle was shot in Shetland back in 1918, according to the charity.

A reintroduction project was started in Scotland in 1975 and the birds have now become established as a self-sustaining population. They returned to the Isle of Mull in the 1980s.

articles.title: 1,300-year-old wallaby teeth found in Queensland with resin still attached reveal how ancient people made necklaces and headbands
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Twelve animal teeth found in a rockshelter in northern Queensland have revealed evidence of a rare form of ancient personal adornment. Discovered at t.
articles.body: Twelve animal teeth found in a rockshelter in northern Queensland have revealed evidence of a rare form of ancient personal adornment. Discovered at the Windmill Way site in southeast Cape York Peninsula, the macropod incisors were found with small balls of plant resin attached to their roots. Radiocarbon dating of two resin samples placed the objects at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 years old. Chemical analysis identified the resin as primarily coming from grass trees, while traces of plant fibre and a fragment of animal hide were also found among the remains. The teeth showed no clear signs of having been used as cutting, scraping or drilling tools. Instead, the arrangement of resin and fibres indicates that they were probably attached to string. Researchers therefore identify the objects as likely components of a necklace or headband. Rock art from nearby Biniirr National Park provides additional evidence for macropod teeth being incorporated into personal ornaments in the region.What did the resin analysis reveal about the 12 wallaby teethChemical analysis showed that the adhesive on all 12 teeth contained compounds consistent with resin from grass trees (Xanthorrhoea). Several samples were specifically consistent with Xanthorrhoea johnsonii, while one tooth also contained compounds associated with Erythrophleum chlorostachys resin. According to the study published in Australian Archaeology, titled ‘An assemblage of resin-mounted macropod incisors from Quinkan Country, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland’, the presence of two resin types on one artefact could indicate that it was reused or repaired, or that the adhesive was deliberately made using two resin sources.The resin was not spread across the teeth in a broad coating. Instead, it formed small, neat balls pressed and smoothed around the extreme root ends. Five teeth also contained plant cellulose fibres associated with the resin, with four showing fibres positioned laterally in a way consistent with string attachment. One tooth contained a small fragment of animal hide embedded in its resin ball. The researchers therefore proposed that the resin balls may have acted as stopping devices, preventing twisted two-ply plant fibre string from slipping towards the root of each tooth.How did researchers identify the wallaby teeth as ancient jewelleryThe researchers found several lines of evidence supporting an interpretation as personal adornment. The teeth showed no convincing use-wear associated with practical tasks, while their resin-mounted roots and traces of plant fibres were consistent with attachment to a string. The study concludes that the 12 incisors were most likely components of a necklace or headband, although it cannot establish whether they belonged to one object or several separate objects.Rock art from two shelters in nearby Biniirr National Park also provides evidence relevant to the interpretation. One motif depicts an anthropomorphic figure with apparent ceremonial regalia, including a headdress containing a series of elongated objects interpreted as possible macropod incisors. Another motif appears to show a necklace made from teeth. The researchers note that these painted representations are approximately 45–50 kilometres northeast of Windmill Way and provide supporting evidence for the use of macropod incisors in personal ornaments in the region.What makes the Windmill Way wallaby teeth discovery significantThe Windmill Way discoveries are significant because organic ornaments are rarely preserved in Australian archaeological sites. The study notes that animal-tooth ornaments have previously been documented mainly in burial contexts, particularly in southeastern Australia, while convincing examples from non-burial archaeological contexts are extremely uncommon. Comparable ornaments include pierced kangaroo teeth and necklaces or headbands incorporating animal teeth.The preservation of the Windmill Way material also allows researchers to identify details that would otherwise have disappeared. More than 500 pieces of plant fibre string had previously been preserved at the site, and the resin on the teeth provided an additional record of organic technology from the pre-contact period. The teeth represent an extremely rare Late Holocene example of personal ornamentation from a non-burial archaeological context in Australia, while the direct dating of the resin provides an age for the objects themselves rather than relying on the age of a burial.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ICC leaders condemn efforts to erode international legal order
articles.summary: Efforts to isolate the International Criminal Court aim to undermine the global rule of law, leaders say.
articles.body:
The current and former presidents of the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) governing body have said that efforts to isolate the institution diplomatically are aimed at eroding confidence in the international legal ⁠order, as US President Donald Trump’s administration has pressured countries to isolate the ICC.

“Efforts to isolate the Court diplomatically – whether by encouraging States Parties to withdraw from the Rome Statute or urging non-States Parties to join measures ⁠intended to weaken it – are aimed at eroding not only one institution, but confidence in the international legal order itself,” Paivi Kaukoranta, the current president of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, and seven former presidents said in a joint op-ed published on Thursday.

In the piece that appeared on the Just Security law and policy journal’s website, they argued that the ICC represented a collective decision by sovereign states to create rules for prosecuting genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The court, they stressed, is not intended to replace national justice systems.

“The ICC is a court of last resort,” the authors wrote.

They also rejected the argument that the court necessarily undermines state sovereignty, saying that countries joining international treaties and institutions are exercising sovereignty rather than surrendering it.

The statement comes as the Trump administration sanctioned ICC judges and officials and pressured countries to distance themselves from the court.

The US, which is not a member of the ICC, has strongly opposed its cases involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and past investigations involving US personnel.

But the current and former assembly presidents framed the dispute more broadly, warning against a world in which political power determines when international law applies.

“The choice before us is between a world based on the rule of law and one where might decides what is right,” they wrote.

They called on the ICC’s 125 member states, international and regional organisations and other supporters of international law to provide the court with political, legal and practical backing and to help governments resist pressure to weaken it. “Now is the time to strengthen the institutions that uphold international law, not dismantle them.”

Washington has sanctioned Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, over what Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as efforts to prompt ICC action against Israeli officials.

The Trump administration has also ended US participation in the UN Human Rights Council, halted funding to UNRWA and withdrawn from UNESCO and the World Health Organization.

In January, Trump ordered the US to leave dozens more international and UN bodies, including UN Women, the UN Population Fund and the UN climate convention, saying they conflicted with US interests and sovereignty.

articles.title: Missouri Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed map from November’s midterms
articles.summary: Republicans have pledged to appeal the ruling to the US Supreme Court with only months until the midterm elections.
articles.body:
The Missouri Supreme Court has unanimously blocked a congressional map backed by United States President Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterm elections, restoring the state’s previous districts.

Thursday’s ruling delivered a rare judicial rebuke to Trump in the national battle over redistricting . But it is unlikely to be the final word in the case, with Republican officials already pledging to appeal the ruling.

At the heart of the case is a congressional map signed into law in September 2025, designed to help Republicans win an extra seat in the US House of Representatives this year.

But the partisan redistricting effort prompted a popular backlash, with nearly 300,000 Missouri residents signing a petition to instead put the new map to a vote.

Missouri’s Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected the petition as legally insufficient. That set up the legal fight, which the Missouri Supreme Court decided on Thursday.

“The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” the court wrote in its ruling.

It added that the Missouri Constitution has made such petitions legal, and “no exception applies”. The court is staffed by seven judges, five of whom are Republican-appointed.

The decision, however, places Missouri in a complicated position. Two months remain until the midterm elections, and ballots will soon be printed.

There are also outstanding legal questions over whether a state’s general election can use different congressional districts than its primaries did.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said she would immediately appeal the ruling to the US Supreme Court. She called Thursday’s decision a “full-fledged constitutional crisis”.

“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election,” she said in a statement.

Trump also denounced the ruling in a social media post , calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional”.

“The Missouri Supreme Court just ridiculously ruled in favor of changing the maps back to what they were a long time ago. It’s called, Ancient History,” he wrote.

Last year, Trump triggered the nationwide redistricting fight when he approached Texas state lawmakers to redraw their maps in a way that would give Republicans an advantage.

Normally, congressional maps are redrawn once every 10 years to reflect census results.

But Trump encouraged Republican-led states to issue new maps mid-decade, as a strategy to help the right-wing party maintain control over the House.

Some 10 states ultimately decided to redistrict, including Missouri. Most tilted in favour of Republicans. California, meanwhile, redrew its map to skew Democratic.

Prior to Thursday’s ruling, Missouri’s Supreme Court affirmed that the special legislative action to change the state’s congressional map was lawful. In the US, no federal law bars partisan redistricting, known as gerrymandering.

But Thursday’s decision upheld the legality of the petition campaign to put the map up for a vote.

The Missouri Supreme Court barred the 2025 map from being used in November’s midterm election or any future election until Missouri voters approve it first.

The group People Not Politicians spearheaded the referendum petition. In a statement on Thursday, it applauded the state court’s decision, which overturned a lower court ruling.

“Supreme Court of Missouri has ruled: Missourians will vote on politicians’ rigged map,” the group wrote on social media.

It also blamed Missouri’s secretary of state for any hurdles to restoring the old map.

“Hoskins had the power to prevent all this confusion months ago — and he chose not to,” the group said.

A day before the court’s ruling, hundreds of people rallied outside the state Supreme Court, chanting: “Let us vote!”

Grant Christensen, a resident of Jefferson City and referendum supporter, said he had signed the petition.

“Gerrymandering is the same as voter suppression,” Christensen said. “Cutting up districts in order to steer them to vote one way or the other is not fair.”

Missouri’s 2025 congressional map had already shaped the state’s primary elections. Critics, however, point out that Hoskins did not reject the referendum until August 4, the day of the party primaries.

The outcome of the legal battle is likely to be most pivotal for Missouri’s 5th congressional district, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver. His district, which encompasses parts of Kansas City, was reshaped to favour Republicans.

articles.title: Two men rescued from flood-stricken Nepali power plant where scores feared trapped
articles.summary: Two people have been rescued from inside the tunnels of a stricken Nepali hydropower plant, and voices have been heard, nine days after massive flash floods and landslides trapped hundreds of workers inside multiple Himalayan energy projects.
articles.body: Two people have been rescued from inside the tunnels of a stricken Nepali hydropower plant, and voices have been heard, nine days after massive flash floods and landslides trapped hundreds of workers inside multiple Himalayan energy projects. In a dramatic breakthrough for what has been a desperate, round-the-clock rescue effort in treacherous conditions, the two men were pulled in quick succession from inside the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant, where an operation has been underway to bore into a tunnel to search for 42 workers that were unaccounted for. Video showed about a dozen rescuers pulling a man from a small hole in the ground and clapping as he reached safety. “Rescuers heard voices,” Bipin Regmi, police chief in the flood-hit district of Nuwakot told CNN, adding a medical team was on its way to the site. The tunnel that leads to the underground powerhouse there, where dozens of people were working when the catastrophic flood hit, is more than four kilometers (2.5 miles) long. Hopes had been fading for the safe rescue of the workers at the plants that run along Nepal’s Trishuli River – among them foreigners from China, South Korea and India. A torrent of cement-like floodwater had engulfed the river and its surrounding areas, killing more than 1,200 people in Nepal. It’s not clear how many people may still be alive inside the tunnel where the rescue effort is unfolding. Nepali authorities say there are more than 900 workers missing at multiple energy projects in the Himalayas including many foreign national workers. Parikshit Mehra, an Indian army colonel, told CNN’s Anderson Cooper, who reported from the Trishuli 3A site earlier this week, that for a rescue mission like this one, “the first 48 hours are the most crucial.” “People who are stuck tend to panic much more than when they are outside in the open,” Mehra said in an interview with Cooper earlier this week, outside the tunnels where the colonel was leading a team of specialized troops. “Getting stuck in a tunnel you can’t see anything. Generally if you stay in the dark you get disoriented in about 24-25 hours,” he said. “Beyond that, (after) 48 hours, you start hallucinating. And then I think from there on it’s always a fight.” But, Mehra added: “There have been miracles.”

articles.title: Rescues underway as two men pulled alive from Nepal hydro tunnel more than a week after flooding
articles.summary: The dramatic breakthrough comes after voices were heard from inside the tunnels of the stricken plant. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• Men rescued: Two people have been rescued from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal, a dramatic breakthrough for a desperate, round-the-clock effort in treacherous conditions more than a week after catastrophic floods hit the country’s border with China.

• Voices heard: Rescue operations are underway. A local police chief and a lawmaker said voices have been heard from inside the tunnels of the stricken plant, after the disaster trapped hundreds of workers inside multiple Himalayan energy projects.

• “World first”: A disaster-response expert advising the rescue efforts described the operation as a dangerous and unprecedented attempt to identify buried tunnel entrances. He said the hydropower tunnels were “full of water” in the aftermath of the floods.

• Death toll: The number of people killed in Nepal following the flash floods now exceeds 1,290.

As water, concrete and debris stormed through the darkness, almost sweeping him off his feet, Ram Chandra tightly gripped onto one of the rungs studded into the roof of the tunnel he was working in on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli river.

His quick reaction likely saved his life, in an earlier extraordinary rescue at the tunnels five days ago.

“The water was rising and it was difficult to move my legs. If I had let go from that rung I would have fallen,” Chandra told a CNN team on the ground after being brought down from the disaster zone by helicopter on Sunday.

He had grabbed hold of a tin sheet to have something to place under his feet and the group passed it around as they inched their way forward, rung by rung, for six hours.

“There were six of us and we later found someone else at the gate of the tunnel,” he said.

Arnold Dix, a disaster-response expert and tunnel engineering professor advising the rescue efforts, described the operation as a dangerous and unprecedented attempt to identify buried tunnel entrances.

“It appears we now have proof of concept for a methodology to perform a rescue, because this is a world first,” he said from Singapore, en route to Nepal.

“We’ve never done this before, and now we have a proof. And there’s other power stations we still haven’t got to.”

“Of course, we pause and celebrate. But it now also means we need to take a back step and go, ‘Okay, of the 500 reasons we all thought we could fail, we’ve been able to prove one method that works. Now, how can we apply that somewhere else?’” he told CNN.

Dix described the hydropower tunnels left as “full of water” in the aftermath of the floods. Teams have to make the high-risk decisions to blow up “rocks the size of cars” to reach people trapped inside, he said.

“So we’re tunneling along under the roof, and we know in our heads that underneath us are likely people who died. So there’s a whole lot of psychology and all of that,” he said.

There were 42 people missing at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where two people were pulled alive from a tunnel Friday, according to a Nepal Army list released on Thursday morning local time.

More than 900 workers in total are still considered missing at 11 different hydro schemes in Nepal.

“Getting stuck in a tunnel you can’t see anything. Generally if you stay in the dark you get disoriented in about 24-25 hours,” he said. “Beyond that, (after) 48 hours, you start hallucinating. And then I think from there on it’s always a fight.”

But, Mehra added: “There have been miracles.”

For context: Today’s rescues took place nine days after the disaster struck, underscoring how significant this breakthrough is. However there are some 900 workers missing inside the tunnels at multiple energy projects in the Himalayas.

A second person has now been rescued from inside the tunnels of the stricken Nepali hydropower plant, Bipin Regmi, police chief for the district of Nuwakot, told CNN.

Shri Ram Neupane, a local lawmaker, confirmed the rescue on Facebook and posted a picture of the man lying on a stretcher with an oxygen mask on his face.

Cheers erupted as a man was pulled alive from a tunnel at Nepal’s Trishuli 3A Hydropower project on Friday morning, after being trapped inside for nine days after catastrophic floods tore through the region.

Video showed the man being hoisted by a group of rescuers from a hole bored down into the tunnel, as onlookers clapped and cheered.

Dozens of hydropower worker are believed to have been near the powerhouse inside the tunnel when the disaster stuck last Wednesday.

“Rescuers heard voices,” said Bipin Regmi, police chief in the flood-hit district of Nuwakot told CNN, adding a medical team was on its way to the site.

articles.title: Missionaries are still going to Africa. But for African Christian leaders, it is the West that needs help
articles.summary: Two years ago, Nigerian pastor Jerry Eze arrived in London to lead a prayer conference at Twickenham — the world’s largest rugby stadium — and immediately wondered whether he had picked the wrong place.
articles.body: Two years ago, Nigerian pastor Jerry Eze arrived in London to lead a prayer conference at Twickenham — the world’s largest rugby stadium — and immediately wondered whether he had picked the wrong place. The event had yet to begin, and the 82,000-seat arena appeared even larger than he had imagined, with rows of empty seats stretching out before him. But as the start time approached, worshippers began to arrive, filling the seats one by one. Soon, the vast stadium was packed — not with rugby fans or concertgoers, but with thousands who came to pray with an African preacher. When Eze stepped onto the stage and faced the crowd, he told CNN he felt a mix of nerves and gratitude — praying he would fulfill what he believed was God’s purpose for him there. Eze reaches a global audience through daily prayer broadcasts on YouTube. To him, what happened at Twickenham showed how Christianity is changing around the world. For generations, Christian mission flowed primarily from Europe and North America to Africa. Missionaries often arrived alongside European militaries, closely linking Christian mission with colonial rule in the minds of many Africans. Their presence is still felt – the United States remains the world’s largest missionary-sending country by far, according to the World Christian Database. Only last month, American missionary Kevin Rideout was released after nine months in captivity in Niger, where he worked with SIM International, a Christian mission organization that has operated in the country for more than 100 years. But now the traffic is two-way. A new generation of African Christians is challenging that old pattern, spreading the gospel in the opposite direction. “When I was growing up, the common picture of a missionary was a Westerner coming to Africa,” Tshepang Basupi, the Southern Africa director of Africa Inland Mission, told CNN. “Today, we have Africans going to other parts of Africa, to Asia, to Europe and to North America.” Basupi, who is from Botswana, leads more than 100 missionaries and helps recruit Africans for cross-cultural mission work. Many are finding their style of preaching is highly popular among the African diaspora in Europe and North America, where they satisfy a hunger for a different kind of Christianity. Rather than bringing a new religion to a population, these missionaries are bringing a new style of religion to places they see as having lost the fervor that they see at home. Eze describes himself as “a missionary to the West,” and says this influence comes partly from the way Africans practice Christianity. “For us here in Africa, it is the fervency and the zeal with which we do it. There’s an African passion and stamina,” he said, adding, “the fire is leaving the West.” From Africa to the world This movement is not new, but it has grown as Christianity spreads in Africa. In 2008, about 18,400 African missionaries had served abroad, according to one estimate. Although more recent data is not available for direct comparison, a 2024 report by the Lausanne Movement, using World Christian Database data, found that missionary activity is now much more global, with Nigeria alone sending an estimated 20,000 missionaries abroad in 2020. CAPRO, a mission group from Nigeria, says it has over 800 missionaries from more than 27 countries working in 46 nations worldwide, including Canada, where its teams evangelize among indigenous communities. Dondo Iorlamen, the international director of CAPRO, believes Africa is well-positioned to send missionaries because Christianity is growing stronger there. “Africa and Asia are the leading mission-sending regions in the world,” he said. The mission is not only about bringing people back to faith. Some African Christians also see it as a way of restoring Christian values they believe the West has moved away from. Harvey Kwiyani, a Malawian theologian based in England who studies African Christianity and its role in the West, said this includes conservative views on sexuality, as well as differences over everyday life, such as going to pubs, which some African Pentecostals consider incompatible with Christian life. “The Africans are coming in to re-evangelize Westerners so they can go back to what they consider Christian values,” he told CNN. But Kwiyani is skeptical about how successful that effort will be. He says the West has, to a great extent, “moved on from Christianity,” and many people there no longer consider themselves religious. “Christianity itself is a very demanding religion,” he said. “It requires you to sort of shift your culture so you can be shaped by this golden spirit that most Westerners don’t really want to deal with at the moment.” The growing movement of African Christians into the West is sometimes described as “reverse mission.” But Basupi rejects that idea. “‘Reverse mission’ assumes that mission belongs to the West and that Africa is simply reversing the direction of Western missionary movement,” he said. “Mission is not for the West only; it is for every believer.” Why the West? Eze says African missions are increasingly looking to the West because many churches there are shrinking and fewer people identify as religious. The decline is visible across Europe. A 2025 Pew study found that 67% of people in Europe were Christian in 2020, compared with 75% in 2010. In North America, 63% were Christian in 2020, versus 77% in 2010. The US has also seen a decline in the number of Christians. Pew’s latest Religious Landscape Study found that 62% of US adults identified as Christian in 2023-24, while 29% had no religious affiliation. In sub-Saharan Africa, the number of Christians grew 31% between 2010 and 2020, reaching 697 million, according to Pew. It is now home to the world’s largest Christian population. Eze sees those changes as evidence of a spiritual need that African Christians can help address. “These are the people who showed us God,” he said. “But Christianity is declining there.” He believes “the baton of revival is in Africa right now” — and that African Christianity has something the West needs. “God has given us something we call the miraculous. It is our currency. It is something they are looking for,” he said, describing a strong emphasis many African Christians place on prayer, healing and the supernatural. Nigerian pastor William Kumuyi, whose Global Crusades have taken his ministry to countries across several continents, sees those qualities as a wider feature of African Christianity. “Christianity in Africa is characterized by unreserved faith, fervent prayer, and reliance on God’s supernatural intervention,” he said, adding that African churches can offer Western societies “a rekindled passion for the authority of Scripture, holiness of life, and expectancy for miracles.” But reaching the West doesn’t always mean reaching large numbers of Westerners. African churches in the West often serve migrant communities. A 2021 study by the World Council of Churches found that migration is contributing to the growth of minority churches in some European countries. “They are not growing among the Whites. They are growing among the migrants, especially Africans,” said Iorlamen. Eze, whose ministry has churches in the US, UK, and Canada, said many who attend his conferences are Black, but some are White as well. Kumuyi said the goal is to reach beyond diaspora communities. “While diaspora communities often provide an initial entry point, our clear objective is never to build ethnic enclaves,” he said. “In the Canadian cities of Granby, Toronto, and Hamilton, as well as outreaches across Asia and Oceania, the focus is the broader host population.” A changing mission, with old baggage The changing direction of Christian mission is also challenging the old idea of what a “missionary” is. Iorlamen says the word still carries the weight of Africa’s colonial past. “Some people don’t like it,” he said. “It reminds them of colonialism and the offenses some missionaries committed — conniving with the colonial masters to enslave people.” Basupi says the growing role of African Christians in global mission does not mean Western missionaries are no longer needed in Africa. “There is room for everyone,” he said. “We should come as equal partners and fellow servants, learning from one another and contributing where we are needed.” Two years after Twickenham, Eze is preparing to return to Britain for a conference at Manchester’s Old Trafford stadium, with nearly 100,000 people registered, he said. Whether that reflects a revival among Western populations or the strength of Africa’s Christian diaspora, Eze sees it as a new chapter. “They preached God to us. We accepted Him and wanted to know Him. Now, we’re going back to show them what He can do.”

articles.title: Steve Irwin's family celebrates 'superhero' dad, 20 years after shock death
articles.summary: The Australian icon was killed in 2006, after a stingray's barb pierced his chest during filming.
articles.body:
Australian conservationist Bindi Irwin has marked the 20th anniversary of her famous father's death with a touching tribute to the man best known as the "Crocodile Hunter".

Steve Irwin died on 4 September 2006, aged 44, after a stingray fatally pierced his chest while he was underwater filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.

Bindi, who was eight when her father died, called Steve a "superhero" in an online post on Friday, saying she has "watched the world mourn my dad with our family" for the past two decades.

"I always thought that my dad's legacy is wildlife conservation; it turns out, his legacy is love. For our planet and for each other," Bindi, 28, wrote on Instagram.

She described the impact of her father's death on her mother Terri and her younger brother Robert, 22.

"My mum lost the love of her life; my brother and I lost the greatest dad," she wrote. "Grief never truly leaves us; we walk alongside it every day."

Bindi also shared details on how her daughter connects with the grandfather she never got to meet.

"I have a 5-year-old daughter who watches his documentaries every morning. She feels utterly loved by her 'grandpa crocodile' without ever having met him."

Since Steve's death, the Irwins have continued to run Australia Zoo in Queensland.

"My dad left a lasting impact so poignant that it will ripple out for generations to come," Bindi wrote, saying his life and legacy were "worth celebrating".

She thanked Steve for being the family's "guardian angel" and signed off her message saying she loved him "with my whole heart".

Steve's wife Terri also took to social media to mark the day, posting an interview where the khaki-clad wildlife advocate recounted Bindi's birth and its impact on him.

"The most incredible wildlife encounter of my life was the birth of my daughter, Bindi," Steve says in the interview, with his signature enthusiasm.

The first time he held his newborn child, the inspiration for her name hit him.

"I was flabbergasted and it was then that her name evolved. I've gone, 'Bindi!' after my favourite crocodile, Bindi," he said, with a wide grin.

Robert Irwin also posted a tribute to his father, with a photo of Steve holding him when he was a baby, alongside the caption, "Your legacy is forever".

Last November, Robert was crowned the winner of US dance competition Dancing with the Stars, a decade after his sister won the same title.
